title: Compound Components and the Slot Pattern

subChunks.title: Compound Components and the Slot Pattern
subChunks.hookHtml: Some components are naturally a collection of related sub-components: a Select with Option items, a Tabs container with Tab and TabPanel pieces. The compound components pattern lets callers compose these pieces freely while the parent manages shared state — without prop drilling or rigid configuration objects.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The problem with configuration-heavy components

// ❌ Rigid — every option requires a prop:
<Tabs
  tabs={[
    { id: 'overview', label: 'Overview', content: <OverviewPanel /> },
    { id: 'stats', label: 'Stats', content: <StatsPanel /> },
  ]}
  activeTab="overview"
  onTabChange={setActiveTab}
/>

Compound components — flexible composition

// ✅ Composable — caller controls the structure:
<Tabs defaultActive="overview">
  <Tabs.List>
    <Tabs.Tab id="overview">Overview</Tabs.Tab>
    <Tabs.Tab id="stats">Stats</Tabs.Tab>
  </Tabs.List>
  <Tabs.Panel id="overview"><OverviewPanel /></Tabs.Panel>
  <Tabs.Panel id="stats"><StatsPanel /></Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>

Implementation using Context

The parent manages shared state; sub-components read it via context:

const TabsContext = createContext(null);

function Tabs({ defaultActive, children }) {
  const [active, setActive] = useState(defaultActive);

  return (
    <TabsContext.Provider value={{ active, setActive }}>
      <div className="tabs">{children}</div>
    </TabsContext.Provider>
  );
}

function TabList({ children }) {
  return <div className="tab-list" role="tablist">{children}</div>;
}

function Tab({ id, children }) {
  const { active, setActive } = useContext(TabsContext);
  return (
    <button
      role="tab"
      aria-selected={active === id}
      className={active === id ? 'tab tab--active' : 'tab'}
      onClick={() => setActive(id)}
    >
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

function TabPanel({ id, children }) {
  const { active } = useContext(TabsContext);
  if (active !== id) return null;
  return <div role="tabpanel">{children}</div>;
}

// Attach sub-components as properties:
Tabs.List = TabList;
Tabs.Tab = Tab;
Tabs.Panel = TabPanel;

Vex: "The compound components pattern is the library designer's tool. When you're building a component that will be used in many different configurations, give the caller the building blocks instead of trying to anticipate every configuration with props. They know their use case; you don't."

When to use this pattern

  • Components with multiple distinct parts that must share state
  • When callers need control over the ordering or nesting of sub-parts
  • When you're building a reusable component library
  • Accordions, Tabs, Select/Option, Dialog with parts, Menus

storyBeats.text: Vex builds a lantern from modular parts: a glass dome, a flame chamber, a base. Each piece works independently. Together they form a lantern — and the caller decides how tall the base is or whether to add a handle. No single 'build lantern' spell; just composable components.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The parent manages state. The children read it via context. The caller composes them freely. This is how Radix UI, Headless UI, and every serious component library is built — because they can't anticipate every possible use case, so they give you the pieces.

storyBeats.speaker: Tabs compound component
storyBeats.text:
<Tabs defaultActive="one">
  <Tabs.List>
    <Tabs.Tab id="one">Tab One</Tabs.Tab>
    <Tabs.Tab id="two">Tab Two</Tabs.Tab>
  </Tabs.List>
  <Tabs.Panel id="one">Content for tab one</Tabs.Panel>
  <Tabs.Panel id="two">Content for tab two</Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a Tabs compound component system with the API shown in the explanation. Requirements:

  • Tabs — manages active tab state, provides context, data-testid="tabs"
  • Tabs.List — container for tab buttons
  • Tabs.Tab — button that sets active tab; active tab gets className="active" and aria-selected="true"
  • Tabs.Panel — renders children only when its id matches the active tab

guidedPracticeTests.label: Clicking second tab shows second panel

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build an Accordion compound component from scratch using the same pattern. Accordion manages open state. Accordion.Item wraps one entry. Accordion.Trigger toggles open/close. Accordion.Content shows content only when open. Support both single-open and multi-open modes via a multiple prop on the parent.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the compound components pattern to a developer who uses prop-drilling or rigid config objects for multi-part components. What problem does it solve? Walk through how the parent manages state and how sub-components access it without props being passed explicitly.

questions.prompt: How do sub-components in a compound component pattern typically access shared state?
options: Via a Context that the parent provides — sub-components call useContext to read the state
Via props explicitly passed from the parent to each sub-component
Via a global store that all components subscribe to
Via React.cloneElement — the parent injects props into each child
questions.answer: Via a Context that the parent provides — sub-components call useContext to read the state
questions.explanation: The parent creates and provides a Context with its state and setters. Sub-components (Tab, TabPanel, etc.) call useContext to read the shared state. This eliminates prop drilling while keeping the state co-located in the parent.

questions.prompt: Why are sub-components attached to the parent as properties (e.g., `Tabs.Tab = Tab`)?
options: It provides a clear API namespace — users import Tabs and get all related components with dot notation
It's required for React to recognise them as part of the compound component
It shares state between the parent and sub-components automatically
It prevents the sub-components from being used outside the parent
questions.answer: It provides a clear API namespace — users import Tabs and get all related components with dot notation
questions.explanation: Attaching sub-components as properties is a purely ergonomic convention. import { Tabs } from './Tabs' gives you Tabs, Tabs.List, Tabs.Tab, Tabs.Panel — all related components from one import. Sub-components are still normal components; the dot notation is just JavaScript object properties.

questions.prompt: When should you use the compound components pattern vs. a simple config-object prop?
options: Use compound components when callers need control over structure, ordering, or insertion of custom elements between sub-parts
Always use compound components — they are strictly superior to config objects
Use config objects when the component will be used more than once
Use compound components only when the component library requires it
questions.answer: Use compound components when callers need control over structure, ordering, or insertion of custom elements between sub-parts
questions.explanation: Config objects work well for fixed structures: <Tabs tabs={[{id, label, content}]} />. Compound components shine when callers need to insert custom elements between tabs, render tabs conditionally, or mix in other components. If the caller only ever needs the standard layout, a config object is simpler.
